C0.quote: voters can alter the issue-dependent weights of a set of elected representatives
C0.note: Hybrid voting system (elections plus delegation); complexity and simulation analysis of outcomes.

C1.quote: demonstrate empirically that common multi-winner election rules for selecting representatives do not perform well
C1.note: NP-hardness (AL); propositions/theorem on delegation outcomes measured as agreement with the majority (WD); extensive simulations (SI). Simulations make up the largest share.

C2.1.value: preference profile; preferences; approvals or complete rankings; delegations
C2.1.quote: the collective profile of preferences over the issues as a whole is PV

C2.2.quote: Voters can express their electoral preferences PV C as either approvals or complete rankings
C2.2.note: Also normalized cardinal weights for candidates, binary issue preferences, and delegation weights (OTH).

C2.3.quote: On each issue s i , each voter v j has a preference v ij ∈ {0, 1}.

C2.4.quote: Voters express their preferences for each issue s ∈ S.
C2.4.note: Preferences are treated as the input to the rule directly; no statement about sincere reporting. Electoral preferences are derived from issue preferences by assumption.

C3.1.quote: Our analysis also did not examine strategic behavior by the voters, candidates, or representatives

C3.2.note: Preferences are used directly. Rankings and approvals are 'derived exactly' from issue agreement, which is a modelling assumption rather than a sincerity statement.

C4.1.note: The paper does not use utility, welfare or satisfaction for voters in its criteria. 'Social welfare' is mentioned only in future work. Agreement is the metric.

C4.2.note: The term 'dichotomous preferences' is not used for inputs. It appears only in citation titles and 'dichotomous choice'.

C5.1.quote: fraction of issues on which they produce the outcome corresponding to the voter majority
C5.1.note: Agreement with the voter majority is a representation/distortion-like criterion for outcomes with respect to voters.

C5.2.quote: On each issue s i , each voter v j has a preference v ij ∈ {0, 1}.
C5.2.note: Evaluated against voter preferences, which are used directly as the input without any statement relating reports to held attitudes.

VOT.quote_behav: voters delegate incisively to representatives with whom they agree on each individual issue
VOT.note: Voters elect and delegate. Delegation behaviour is fixed by the model (random probability, incisive, Best Rep, etc.) with no optimisation.

CAN.note: Candidates and representatives only have fixed preferences, take no actions in the model, and strategic behaviour is explicitly not examined.

C8.1.note: NA: no type is STRAT or MIXED.

claims.quote: reveal the potential for Flexible Representative Democracy to improve outcomes as voter participation increases
the choice of election rule appears less important than the quality of the electoral candidates
Flexible Representative Democracy provides an alternative taking the best of both worlds

C9.2.quote: our simplistic model is sufficient to show
C9.2.note: The claims need an assumption that voters' preferences and delegations are sincere and incisive, and that Direct Democracy majority outcomes are the ideal. Voter delegation behaviour is stated as a modelling assumption, but sincerity of reported electoral preferences is not stated. Limitations are acknowledged, which partly mitigates this.

C10.1.note: The paper does not state that it takes a procedural-only reading.
